excerpts: This repository contains training scripts to train a text detector based on [manga-image-translator](https://github.com/zyddnys/manga-image-translator) which can extract bounding-boxes, text lines and segmentation of text from manga or comics to help further comics translation procedures such as text-removal, recognition, lettering, etc.

Our current model can be summarized as below. All models were trained on around 13 thousand anime & comic style images, 1/3 from Manga109-s, 1/3 from [DCM](https://digitalcomicmuseum.com/), and 1/3 are synthetic data in a weak supervision manner due to the lack of available high-quality annotations. We used text detection model of manga-image-translator to generate text lines annotations for manga, and [Manga-Text-Segmentation](https://github.com/juvian/Manga-Text-Segmentation) with some post-processing to generate masks for both manga and comics. Synthetic data were generated using around 4k text-free anime-girls pictures from https://t.me/SugarPic, text-rendering, Unet and DBNet training scripts can be found in this repo. Text block detector was trained using [yolov5 official repository](https://github.com/ultralytics/yolov5)

excerpts: How comic book lettering actually works — font choice, balloon shapes for tone, SFX as drawn art, tail attribution, and the signs that separate pro lettering from amateur.
Round (Speech Balloon) Default. Normal dialogue at normal volume. Round or slightly oval, smooth border, single tail to the speaker.
Jagged (Shout Balloon) Border is sharp angled — sawtooth or starburst. Signals shouting, yelling, or impact. Use sparingly; if every balloon is jagged, the comic feels relentless.

Scalloped or Cloud (Thought Balloon) Wavy or cloud-shaped border. Tail is a series of small disconnected circles rather than a continuous line. Signals interior thought or telepathic communication. Rectangular (Caption/Narration) Sharp-cornered rectangle, no tail. Used for narration, time jumps, scene-setting captions, off-panel voice (radio, TV, voiceover). Often colored differently than dialogue balloons to signal a different speaker register. Outline-Only (Whisper) Standard speech-balloon shape with a thin line border and no fill — sometimes dashed. Signals whisper or fading speech.

Balloon Placement on the Page Placement controls reading order. The reader's eye moves left-to-right (right-to-left for manga) through balloons in each panel before moving to the next panel. Three placement rules: balloons sit at the top of the panel when possible (the eye enters there); the first speaker's balloon goes leftmost (rightmost for manga); avoid balloon-over-face whenever possible (covering a character's mouth or eyes is a craft loss). Working letterers spend real time arranging balloons; placement that looks natural in the finished comic was usually iterated 3–5 times in production.

Print Considerations Lettering for print has constraints digital doesn't. Text under 6pt becomes unreadable at trim. Hairline borders (under 0.5pt) drop out at small print sizes. Color text on color backgrounds needs contrast checking — yellow text on white background reads as nothing in CMYK print. Production checks: print a test page at trim, read at arm's length, and confirm every balloon is legible.

Font Choice — The Single Biggest Decision The wrong font kills a comic before any other lettering decision matters. The convention in comics is a face that imitates hand-drawn caps — readable at small sizes, weighted to balance the art, and characterful enough not to feel mechanical.

Working letterers use fonts from foundries like Blambot, Comicraft, or Hassan Otsmane-Elhaou's collection — most offer free starter fonts. Pick one font for dialogue and stick with it for the entire issue; switching fonts mid-issue reads as inconsistent.

Some safe free starting points: Blambot's CCWildWords (the closest to the standard Marvel/DC house style), Komika Hand, or Anime Ace. All read as comic lettering without screaming 'I'm a font'. Size is typically 6–8pt at print scale; readability at small sizes is the test.

What font should I use for my comic? Pick a comic-specific font from Blambot, Comicraft, or similar. Free options include CCWildWords, Komika Hand, and Anime Ace. Do not use Comic Sans (despite the name, it's not a comic lettering font) or generic serif fonts (Times, Garamond) — they read wrong in panels.
Size is typically 6–8pt at print scale; readability at small sizes is the test.
How big should comic lettering be? Typical body dialogue runs 6–8pt at print scale (about 4–5mm cap height). Test at print size: if you can read the text at arm's length, it's correct.
Production checks: print a test page at trim, read at arm's length, and confirm every balloon is legible.

Tail Attribution — Who's Speaking Comic dialogue doesn't use 'he said' / 'she said' attributions like prose. The balloon tail points at the speaker. Working letterers shape the tail carefully — the tail emerges from the balloon, curves naturally toward the speaker's mouth, and terminates near or at the mouth. Bad tails point at the wrong character or at empty space; readers misattribute the dialogue and the scene reads as confusing.

If a speaker is off-panel, the tail extends to the panel edge and the script marks the speaker — '(off-panel)'.

Italic and Bold Variants Lettering uses italics for stress (the word the speaker emphasizes) and bold for higher emphasis. Most comic fonts ship with italic and bold weights matched to the regular. Use them surgically — bold every other word looks panicked; bold one word every couple of panels lands the emphasis.

excerpts: How comic book lettering actually works — font choice, balloon shapes for tone, SFX as drawn art, tail attribution, and the signs that separate pro lettering from amateur.
Round (Speech Balloon) Default. Normal dialogue at normal volume. Round or slightly oval, smooth border, single tail to the speaker.
Jagged (Shout Balloon) Border is sharp angled — sawtooth or starburst. Signals shouting, yelling, or impact. Use sparingly; if every balloon is jagged, the comic feels relentless.

Scalloped or Cloud (Thought Balloon) Wavy or cloud-shaped border. Tail is a series of small disconnected circles rather than a continuous line. Signals interior thought or telepathic communication. Rectangular (Caption/Narration) Sharp-cornered rectangle, no tail. Used for narration, time jumps, scene-setting captions, off-panel voice (radio, TV, voiceover). Often colored differently than dialogue balloons to signal a different speaker register. Outline-Only (Whisper) Standard speech-balloon shape with a thin line border and no fill — sometimes dashed. Signals whisper or fading speech.

Balloon Placement on the Page Placement controls reading order. The reader's eye moves left-to-right (right-to-left for manga) through balloons in each panel before moving to the next panel. Three placement rules: balloons sit at the top of the panel when possible (the eye enters there); the first speaker's balloon goes leftmost (rightmost for manga); avoid balloon-over-face whenever possible (covering a character's mouth or eyes is a craft loss). Working letterers spend real time arranging balloons; placement that looks natural in the finished comic was usually iterated 3–5 times in production.

Print Considerations Lettering for print has constraints digital doesn't. Text under 6pt becomes unreadable at trim. Hairline borders (under 0.5pt) drop out at small print sizes. Color text on color backgrounds needs contrast checking — yellow text on white background reads as nothing in CMYK print. Production checks: print a test page at trim, read at arm's length, and confirm every balloon is legible.

The default renderer now produces overlapping text because I added logic to enlarge the bounding boxes (for the ENG target language, they are typically enlarged by 1.1x). If these enlarged bounding boxes overlap, the rendered text is very likely to overlap as well. I didn't account for this initially, as the probability seemed low. > > Another reason is that I completely removed the default renderer's logic for automatically shrinking the font size to fit the bounding box. I did this because it would make the text unreasonably small; in earlier versions, it could even shrink the text to the point of being invisible. Later, adding a font_size_minimum didn't help; if the text still didn't fit within the bounding box after being shrunk to the minimum font size, it would continue to shrink (which was the case most of the time). Although this prevented overlap, I found the logic to be too flawed. > > font_size_offset is used to fine-tune the overall font size on a page while maintaining the relative size differences between various text regions. For example, if the text size automatically detected by CTD (Comic Text Detector) is smaller than the default, this parameter can be used to adjust it. > > I’m not familiar with manga2eng, but the current issues with the default renderer include: > > Text can overlap. > Text can extend beyond the page boundaries. > In some text regions, delayed line breaks cause the text to noticeably overflow its speech bubble compared to other regions. > With certain fonts, characters stack on top of each other, causing earlier characters to be partially or even fully obscured by later ones.

The gamma and sigma parameters in the split_text_region method should be increased to merge these overlapping bounding boxes. Then, rendering within the merged bounding box can avoid potential overlap issues. Of course, the finally rendered text would also be rotated. > > Previously, rendering was largely restricted to the dark green areas. This worked well for languages suitable for vertical reading, conforming to the original layout, but it was terrible for horizontally read languages. However, now that the default renderer has removed boundary restrictions during rendering, there is a high probability of overlap after rendering even for vertical text in the situation shown in the image above. Therefore, I think it's better to automatically adjust parameters to merge bounding boxes when there is significant overlap. Currently, merging can only be controlled by manually adjusting these parameters. The vast majority of cases with significant bounding box overlap occur because the text recognition model repeatedly creates multiple boxes in the same location. Merging to reduce redundant, overlapping bounding boxes will be more conducive to using multi-modal models to automatically correct OCR errors. > > This approach would minimize text overlap during rendering, rather than trying to find workarounds at the rendering stage. Of course, relevant processing could also be added during rendering to resolve any individual cases of text overlap that might still occur.

content.executive_summary:
- **Separate The Semantic Planes**: comic-text-detector reports text bounding boxes, text lines, and text segmentation, while a speech-balloon model treats balloon pixels, carriers, and tails as a different semantic object [executive_summary[0]] [15] [executive_summary[1]] [21]. Keep `bubble`, `text_instance`, `line`, `translation`, and `render_region` separate -> merge only after evidence says they belong together.
- **Treat Over-Merge As Association Failure**: manga-image-translator exposes optional OCR box merging and `ignore_bubble` controls [executive_summary[2]] [10], while an issue reports overlap after English boxes were enlarged by 1.1x and automatic font shrinking was removed [executive_summary[3]] [20]. Use conservative grouping, explicit split and merge controls, and post-render overlap checks -> do not solve every bad association by globally increasing dilation.
- **Use Masks For Erasure, Not Just Rectangles**: the detector pipeline is designed to provide text segmentation for removal, recognition, and lettering [executive_summary[0]] [15], and inpainting operates on a mask that separates changed pixels from preserved pixels [executive_summary[4]] [16]. Use line masks for source removal -> reserve rectangles for coarse review, fallback fills, and collision tests.
- **Fit To The Bubble, Not Merely The OCR Box**: the default manga-image-translator renderer is based on detected text rather than a true bubble, while its `manga2eng` mode attempts bubble fitting [executive_summary[2]] [10] [executive_summary[2]] [10]. Compute a safe interior from a balloon mask, then shape and wrap translated text against that interior -> never assume source-line bounds are a valid target layout.
- **Treat Camera Translation As A Fast Preview Layer**: Google documents automatic camera language detection, NMT, offline language downloads, higher quality when online, and reduced flicker [executive_summary[5]] [11]. It does not document comic-specific bubble ownership or pixel-level inpainting -> use it for immediate comprehension, not as evidence of professional comic lettering.
- **Make Bubble Shape A Rendering Input**: round balloons conventionally signal normal dialogue, jagged balloons shouting or impact, cloud balloons thoughts, and rectangular balloons narration [executive_summary[6]] [13]. Preserve the tail and the reading direction, and vary padding, font weight, and line strategy by shape -> a single centered-text rule is not enough.
- **Keep A Human-Correctable Path**: an Android overlay translator offers conservative, standard, and aggressive adjacent-box merging, plus manual selection and vertical Japanese handling [executive_summary[7]] [25] [executive_summary[7]] [25] [executive_summary[7]] [25]. Expose the same controls in a page translator -> ambiguity should become an editable region, not a forced merge or a tiny unreadable font.
content.the_pipeline_why_detection_ocr_translati:
An OCR translator is not one computer-vision problem. It is an association problem across at least four geometries: the pixels containing letters, the text line or block, the balloon or caption that owns the text, and the destination region in which the translation will be drawn. manga-image-translator documents distinct detector, OCR, translator, inpainter, and renderer components [the_pipeline_why_detection_ocr_translation_and_rendering_must_stay_separate[0]] [10] [the_pipeline_why_detection_ocr_translation_and_rendering_must_stay_separate[0]] [10]. comic-text-detector likewise describes outputs for text removal, recognition, and lettering, but its README does not say that those text instances are speech balloons [the_pipeline_why_detection_ocr_translation_and_rendering_must_stay_separate[1]] [15] [the_pipeline_why_detection_ocr_translation_and_rendering_must_stay_separate[1]] [15].

| Stage | What should be retained | Typical failure | Engineering guardrail |
|---|---|---|---|
| Preprocessing | orientation, scale, contrast, crop | vertical or light text is missed | retain the original and record detector parameters; manga-image-translator exposes rotation, inversion, gamma, size, and threshold controls [the_pipeline_why_detection_ocr_translation_and_rendering_must_stay_separate[0]] [10] |
| Text detection | per-line polygon or mask, box, confidence | two lines become one box, or one stylized line becomes many | preserve every primitive before grouping; do not discard line-level candidates |
| Bubble or caption detection | semantic mask, contour, tail, type | two adjacent balloons are treated as one, or a caption is treated as dialogue | run a balloon or caption classifier separately; balloon segmentation is a pixel-wise task and can distinguish captions from speech balloons [the_pipeline_why_detection_ocr_translation_and_rendering_must_stay_separate[2]] [21] [the_pipeline_why_detection_ocr_translation_and_rendering_must_stay_separate[2]] [21] |
| Association | links from lines to blocks and blocks to bubbles | proximity merges unrelated speakers | require same candidate bubble, compatible orientation, and compatible reading order before merging |
| OCR | source text, script, direction, confidence | recognition is run on the wrong crop or broken line order | OCR both the whole candidate bubble and its line crops; manga OCR supports multi-line recognition in one forward pass [the_pipeline_why_detection_ocr_translation_and_rendering_must_stay_separate[3]] [6] |
| Translation | target text plus glossary and line intent | target text is longer, changes emphasis, or loses speaker context | keep source and target as editable records; translate with bubble context, not only isolated fragments |
| Rendering | shaped glyph bounds, safe interior, style, z-order | overflow, overlap, clipped tail, unreadable small text | fit against the destination mask, then run collision and boundary tests |
| Source removal | text mask and background strategy | halos, residual glyphs, damaged line art | use segmentation masks and retain a reversible original |

The key design choice is to delay irreversible operations. OCR can be corrected without rerunning inpainting. A block can be split without losing the original line masks. A translation can be shortened without changing the detector output. Conversely, if a system first unions nearby rectangles, erases the union, and only then asks an OCR or language model to reconstruct structure, it has already destroyed the evidence needed to fix an over-merge.

A practical internal record is therefore: `bubble_id`, `bubble_mask`, `tail_mask`, `bubble_type`, `text_instance_ids`, `line_ids`, `source_text`, `target_text`, `source_direction`, `target_direction`, `safe_mask`, `font`, `font_size`, `line_spacing`, and `render_status`. A line can belong to a block without the block being assigned to a bubble yet. That distinction directly addresses the difference between text-block segmentation and speech-bubble segmentation.
content.manga_image_translator_a_full_page_case_:
manga-image-translator is useful as a reference architecture because it makes the stages visible rather than presenting translation as a single OCR call. Its documentation exposes detector, OCR, translator, inpainter, colorizer, upscaler, and renderer components [manga_image_translator_a_full_page_case_study_in_detection_masking_inpainting_and_rendering[0]] [10] [manga_image_translator_a_full_page_case_study_in_detection_masking_inpainting_and_rendering[0]] [10]. Detector controls include text thresholds, box thresholds, unclip ratio, rotation, inversion, gamma correction, and detection size [manga_image_translator_a_full_page_case_study_in_detection_masking_inpainting_and_rendering[0]] [10]. This is a good operational lesson: a missed vertical line, a false positive from a sound effect, and a bad target-language layout are different knobs and should not be debugged as one model failure.

The project also exposes the central grouping trade-off. Its OCR options include `ignore_bubble`, with a documented range of 1 to 50 and a recommendation of 5 to 10, and `use_mocr_merge` for bounding-box merging during Manga OCR inference [manga_image_translator_a_full_page_case_study_in_detection_masking_inpainting_and_rendering[0]] [10]. Those controls are useful, but they do not turn text boxes into semantic balloon objects. A production implementation should preserve the unmerged boxes and attach a merge explanation, such as same balloon mask, normalized gap, common orientation, and compatible baseline. The issue history reinforces this caution: #974 concerns `textline_merge`, and #1112 reports all DeepL output merged into one line [manga_image_translator_a_full_page_case_study_in_detection_masking_inpainting_and_rendering[1]] [18] [manga_image_translator_a_full_page_case_study_in_detection_masking_inpainting_and_rendering[1]] [18].

Removal is treated as a mask problem. The documentation describes `mask_dilation_offset`, kernel size, inpainting model, inpainting size, and precision; it notes that larger inpainting size can reduce incomplete coverage and source-text leakage, while a larger kernel expands context at some cost to removal accuracy [manga_image_translator_a_full_page_case_study_in_detection_masking_inpainting_and_rendering[0]] [10] [manga_image_translator_a_full_page_case_study_in_detection_masking_inpainting_and_rendering[0]] [10] [manga_image_translator_a_full_page_case_study_in_detection_masking_inpainting_and_rendering[0]] [10]. `lama_large` is the recommended inpainter [manga_image_translator_a_full_page_case_study_in_detection_masking_inpainting_and_rendering[0]] [10]. This is a sensible default for complex art, but it should not be applied blindly to every white balloon. A flat bubble can be cleared with a deterministic fill, which is faster and easier to audit.

Lettering is where a detector-centered design shows its limit. The renderer exposes alignment, font border, font-size offset and minimum, direction, line spacing, hyphenation, color, and RTL controls [manga_image_translator_a_full_page_case_study_in_detection_masking_inpainting_and_rendering[0]] [10]. `manga2eng` attempts to fit translated text to a detected bubble [manga_image_translator_a_full_page_case_study_in_detection_masking_inpainting_and_rendering[0]] [10], but the default renderer's area is determined by detected text rather than actual bubble geometry and therefore cannot guarantee ideal English typesetting [manga_image_translator_a_full_page_case_study_in_detection_masking_inpainting_and_rendering[0]] [10]. The recommended adaptation is to add an independently detected bubble mask and make that mask the destination constraint. Keep manga-image-translator's detector and inpainting stages, but replace implicit proximity merging with an explicit bubble ownership graph and replace box-only fitting with mask-aware layout.
content.comic_text_detector_precise_text_geometr:
comic-text-detector's own README describes three useful outputs: bounding boxes, text lines, and segmentation of text [comic_text_detector_precise_text_geometry_not_bubble_ownership[0]] [15]. It is trained as a text detector based on manga-image-translator and is intended to support text removal, recognition, and lettering [comic_text_detector_precise_text_geometry_not_bubble_ownership[0]] [15]. The repository documentation describes a YOLOv5 text-block detector and training material involving text rendering, U-Net segmentation, and DBNet [comic_text_detector_precise_text_geometry_not_bubble_ownership[0]] [15]. These are valuable outputs for a translator, especially when the original lettering is rotated, irregular, or too close to another line.

The important negative finding is just as useful: the README does not document automatic speech-balloon detection, text-line grouping into balloons, or a semantic owner for each text line [comic_text_detector_precise_text_geometry_not_bubble_ownership[0]] [15] [comic_text_detector_precise_text_geometry_not_bubble_ownership[0]] [15]. Therefore, CTD should be treated as a text-instance and text-mask component, not as a complete speech-bubble detector. Calling a CTD box a bubble causes exactly the failure in the question: two nearby balloons may be merged because their text boxes are close, while one balloon with separated emphasis lines may be split into unrelated translation units.

A separate speech-balloon model provides the missing semantic layer. Dubray and Laubrock frame balloon localization as pixel-wise semantic segmentation, using a U-Net-like network with a VGG-16 encoder [comic_text_detector_precise_text_geometry_not_bubble_ownership[1]] [21] [comic_text_detector_precise_text_geometry_not_bubble_ownership[1]] [21]. Their model includes the carrier and tail, handles varied shapes, and distinguishes speech balloons from captions [comic_text_detector_precise_text_geometry_not_bubble_ownership[1]] [21] [comic_text_detector_precise_text_geometry_not_bubble_ownership[1]] [21]. The paper also explains why the distinction matters: balloons typically carry direct speech or thoughts, whereas captions serve narrative functions, even though both contain text [comic_text_detector_precise_text_geometry_not_bubble_ownership[1]] [21].

| Question | CTD-style text detector | Balloon or caption detector | Recommended decision |
|---|---|---|---|
| What is segmented? | text instances and lines [comic_text_detector_precise_text_geometry_not_bubble_ownership[0]] [15] | balloon or caption pixels, possibly carrier and tail [comic_text_detector_precise_text_geometry_not_bubble_ownership[1]] [21] | retain both masks |
| What is recognized? | letters and line geometry | speech, thought, caption, or other region type | use region type as translation context |
| What does proximity mean? | nearby text may be a candidate group | shared balloon mask is stronger ownership evidence | never merge on distance alone |
| What is the removal mask? | tight text mask | balloon interior or text-only mask, depending on strategy | use text mask for selective removal and bubble mask for safe layout |

The older sift-ocr project shows a practical alternative for simple pages. It flood-fills closed, mostly uniform speech bubbles, crops each mask, reruns OCR, and groups text blocks by y-coordinate and then x-coordinate [comic_text_detector_precise_text_geometry_not_bubble_ownership[2]] [17] [comic_text_detector_precise_text_geometry_not_bubble_ownership[2]] [17]. It measures font size, line spacing, colors, and bounding boxes before repainting translated text [comic_text_detector_precise_text_geometry_not_bubble_ownership[2]] [17] [comic_text_detector_precise_text_geometry_not_bubble_ownership[2]] [17]. Its assumptions are explicit: closed solid boundaries and mostly uniform backgrounds [comic_text_detector_precise_text_geometry_not_bubble_ownership[2]] [17]. The project also warns that noise can corrupt the bounding rectangle and produce malformed text [comic_text_detector_precise_text_geometry_not_bubble_ownership[2]] [17]. That makes flood fill a useful fast path, not a universal solution for open, spiky, textured, or overlapping balloons.
content.google_translate_lens_versus_open_source:
Google's official description of Instant Camera Translation confirms a fast camera pipeline: the app automatically detects the language and translates it [google_translate_lens_versus_open_source_android_workflows[0]] [11], uses Neural Machine Translation, supports downloadable language models, and can use the network for higher quality [google_translate_lens_versus_open_source_android_workflows[0]] [11]. It also reports work to reduce flicker and distinguishes live camera translation from Scan and Import modes [google_translate_lens_versus_open_source_android_workflows[0]] [11]. Google ML Kit similarly describes on-device processing as fast for camera input and usable offline for images and text [google_translate_lens_versus_open_source_android_workflows[1]] [8].

What this public material does not establish is equally important. It does not specify a speech-balloon detector, a bubble ownership graph, an inpainting model, or a comic-lettering algorithm. The correct engineering comparison is therefore not "Google uses method X for bubbles" but "Google supplies a polished region-translation experience whose internal comic layout method is not publicly specified here." Use it as a comprehension benchmark and latency target, not as a transparent implementation recipe.

The strongest open-source Android example found is ciddwd/overlay-translator. Its documented flow is screenshot -> local or cloud OCR -> LLM or machine translation -> floating-window overlay [google_translate_lens_versus_open_source_android_workflows[2]] [25]. It supports local ML Kit OCR and other OCR choices, lets the user choose local or remote services, and explicitly targets games, visual novels, and manga [google_translate_lens_versus_open_source_android_workflows[2]] [25]. It provides conservative, standard, and aggressive adjacent-box merge strengths [google_translate_lens_versus_open_source_android_workflows[2]] [25], supports vertical Japanese, and follows source position and reading direction [google_translate_lens_versus_open_source_android_workflows[2]] [25] [google_translate_lens_versus_open_source_android_workflows[2]] [25]. Its output is a screen overlay or a saved translated image; it is not described as rewriting the original pixels [google_translate_lens_versus_open_source_android_workflows[2]] [25].

| Workflow | Detection and translation scope | Rendering primitive | Best use | Main risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Google camera | automatic camera language detection and NMT [google_translate_lens_versus_open_source_android_workflows[0]] [11] | public description does not specify bubble-aware rendering | quick reading and preview | little control over bubble ownership or typography |
| ciddwd overlay-translator | screenshot OCR, local/cloud engines, manga-oriented ordering [google_translate_lens_versus_open_source_android_workflows[2]] [25] [google_translate_lens_versus_open_source_android_workflows[2]] [25] | floating overlay, with selectable merge strength [google_translate_lens_versus_open_source_android_workflows[2]] [25] | live Android reading | source remains underneath; aggressive merging can over-associate |
| BubbleTranslate | local OCR plus open-source MT for comic/webtoon speech bubbles [google_translate_lens_versus_open_source_android_workflows[3]] [7] [google_translate_lens_versus_open_source_android_workflows[3]] [7] | HTML5 canvas/SVG overlay and original toggle [google_translate_lens_versus_open_source_android_workflows[3]] [7] [google_translate_lens_versus_open_source_android_workflows[3]] [7] | private browser reading | it is a browser extension, not an Android implementation |
| meangrinch MangaTranslator | YOLO and SAM speech-bubble segmentation plus LLM OCR [google_translate_lens_versus_open_source_android_workflows[4]] [3] | inpaint bubbles and outside-bubble text, then render custom fonts [google_translate_lens_versus_open_source_android_workflows[4]] [3] | batch web translation | more compute and more irreversible pixel changes |
| Georgescutelnicu tool | YOLOv8 bubble detection, Manga OCR, OpenCV, and translation services [google_translate_lens_versus_open_source_android_workflows[5]] [4] | clear bubbles, then add translated text into the image [google_translate_lens_versus_open_source_android_workflows[5]] [4] | small Python experiments | documentation does not promise robust ownership or layout |

The platform decision follows from the table. For a live Android reader, use reversible overlays, user-adjustable merge strength, and region handles. For a clean export, use text and balloon masks, background reconstruction, and a renderer that can be checked at final resolution.
content.fitting_translated_text_into_rounded_spi:
A source text box is not a destination box. Translation can change word count, glyph widths, punctuation, line count, and direction. A robust fitter should first define a safe mask, for example `safe = erode(balloon_mask - tail_mask, padding)`, and only then choose a font and line breaks. The tail is not free whitespace: it identifies the speaker and should remain visible. Comic lettering guidance says the tail should point toward the speaker and terminate near the mouth; a wrong tail can cause dialogue misattribution [fitting_translated_text_into_rounded_spiky_and_irregular_balloons[0]] [13].

The fitter should shape the target string with the actual font, measure glyph ink bounds rather than nominal character counts, and search for the largest readable font that satisfies all constraints. For each candidate font size, wrap by available width on each scanline of the safe mask, not by one rectangular width. Score candidates by overflow, unused area, line imbalance, and deviation from the source reading direction. If no candidate fits above the minimum size, shorten or retranslate the sentence, or expose an edit control. Shrinking indefinitely is not a successful fit.

| Balloon or region | Semantic signal | Layout policy | Failure to flag |
|---|---|---|---|
| Round or oval | normal dialogue [fitting_translated_text_into_rounded_spiky_and_irregular_balloons[0]] [13] | center the text; use an eroded oval mask; let upper and lower lines taper naturally | text is mathematically centered but optically too high or too wide |
| Jagged or spiky | shouting, yelling, or impact [fitting_translated_text_into_rounded_spiky_and_irregular_balloons[0]] [13] | preserve points and tail, add larger inner padding, use a stronger but readable face, and avoid filling the spikes | ordinary dialogue styling changes the intended tone |
| Cloud or scalloped | thought or telepathy [fitting_translated_text_into_rounded_spiky_and_irregular_balloons[0]] [13] | use softer spacing and a generous safe interior; do not let lines touch the scallops | text collides with the irregular edge |
| Rectangular caption | narration, time jump, scene setting, or off-panel voice [fitting_translated_text_into_rounded_spiky_and_irregular_balloons[0]] [13] | use caption alignment and margins rather than an oval centering rule | caption is treated as a speaker balloon |
| Sound effect | drawn visual sound, not ordinary dialogue [fitting_translated_text_into_rounded_spiky_and_irregular_balloons[0]] [13] | use a separate SFX renderer with shape, angle, weight, and color controls | OCR translation turns expressive art into a tiny paragraph |

Reading order is part of layout, not an afterthought. The lettering guide places the first speaker's balloon leftmost in left-to-right comics and rightmost for manga, with balloon placement guiding the eye [fitting_translated_text_into_rounded_spiky_and_irregular_balloons[0]] [13]. Preserve source order as a separate field, then render the target in the target language's direction. manga-image-translator already exposes direction, alignment, line spacing, minimum font size, and hyphenation controls [fitting_translated_text_into_rounded_spiky_and_irregular_balloons[1]] [10]; these should be driven by the bubble mask and region type rather than one page-wide default.

A practical implementation uses three passes. Pass one produces a preview with outlines for the bubble, tail, text instances, and safe mask. Pass two searches font size and line breaks, rejecting any candidate whose glyph mask leaves the safe region or intersects another rendered region. Pass three rasterizes the chosen layout, runs an AABB and pixel-mask collision check, and marks the region for review if it overflows. This directly addresses the issue report that enlarged boxes, delayed line breaks, and removed font shrinking can cause overlap, page overflow, and glyph stacking [fitting_translated_text_into_rounded_spiky_and_irregular_balloons[2]] [20].
content.inpainting_versus_overlay_backgrounds:
Inpainting and overlay are not interchangeable outputs. Inpainting changes pixels inside a mask while leaving the rest of the image unchanged; standard inpainting documentation describes the mask as the boundary between the region to fill and the region to preserve [inpainting_versus_overlay_backgrounds[0]] [16] [inpainting_versus_overlay_backgrounds[0]] [16]. An overlay instead adds a new layer, often with a bubble-shaped opaque or translucent background, without requiring the source art to be permanently rewritten.

| Strategy | Best when | Strength | Failure mode | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Deterministic solid or sampled fill | bubble interior is flat white or nearly uniform | fast, reproducible, easy to inspect | wrong color or a visible rectangular edge | use the bubble mask, sample local color, feather only the boundary |
| Local structure or LaMa inpainting | text crosses textured art, line art, or a nonwhite balloon | removes source glyphs while reconstructing context; manga-image-translator exposes Lama and mask-size controls [inpainting_versus_overlay_backgrounds[1]] [10] [inpainting_versus_overlay_backgrounds[1]] [10] | mask leakage, altered line art, or source remnants when coverage is poor | retain the original and compare a high-quality and fast pass |
| Bubble-shaped opaque overlay | live reading or uncertain detection | reversible and low latency; can be moved or removed | source text may show through, and a patch can hide art | use only after source text is hidden by an accurate mask; expose opacity and resize |
| Canvas or floating-screen overlay | Android/browser preview | no destructive rewrite; ciddwd documents floating overlays [inpainting_versus_overlay_backgrounds[2]] [25] and BubbleTranslate draws canvas/SVG overlays [inpainting_versus_overlay_backgrounds[3]] [7] | text can drift with scrolling, cover controls, or misalign after scaling | use for live preview and manual correction |
| Full rewritten export | final translated page | stable image with no dependency on a runtime layer; meangrinch documents inpainting then rendering [inpainting_versus_overlay_backgrounds[4]] [3] | mistakes are harder to undo and need more compute | use only after region and layout QA |

The hybrid policy is strongest. First, preserve the original. Second, use a text mask to remove glyphs. Third, choose a deterministic fill for flat interiors and inpainting for complex backgrounds. Fourth, render the translation on a separate layer before compositing. The sift-ocr experience supports this conditional approach: flood fill works well when balloon boundaries are closed and backgrounds are uniform, but those assumptions fail on many real pages [inpainting_versus_overlay_backgrounds[5]] [17].

Avoid the common mistake of placing a white rectangle over a rounded balloon. It creates an artificial shape, clips the tail, and can cover nearby art. Conversely, avoid inpainting an entire balloon when only text needs removal: the model may unnecessarily change the balloon border or background. The correct mask depends on the output goal: text-only removal for selective repair, the balloon interior for a clean re-lettered bubble, or an overlay region for a reversible live view.
content.community_failure_cases_and_a_practical_:
The most useful community evidence is not a claim that one algorithm always wins; it is the concrete failure vocabulary in issue reports. The manga-image-translator issue list includes #1112, "all Deepl translation output merged into single line," #1029, "Text positioning is incorrect in rendered speech bubbles," and #974, a `textline_merge` error [community_failure_cases_and_a_practical_qa_checklist[0]] [18] [community_failure_cases_and_a_practical_qa_checklist[0]] [18] [community_failure_cases_and_a_practical_qa_checklist[0]] [18]. These titles map directly to three different bugs: translation aggregation, destination placement, and detection/grouping.

Issue #978 gives a more detailed case study. The report says enlarged English bounding boxes can overlap and that the renderer had removed automatic font shrinking, leading to overlap, page overflow, delayed line-break overflow, and stacked characters [community_failure_cases_and_a_practical_qa_checklist[1]] [20]. The discussion proposes increasing `gamma` and `sigma` in `split_text_region`, merging boxes with significant overlap, and adding rendering-time protection [community_failure_cases_and_a_practical_qa_checklist[1]] [20]. It also says merging is currently controlled by manually adjusted parameters and records the maintainer position that translation quality takes priority over layout, with the change closed as not planned [community_failure_cases_and_a_practical_qa_checklist[1]] [20] [community_failure_cases_and_a_practical_qa_checklist[1]] [20] [community_failure_cases_and_a_practical_qa_checklist[1]] [20]. The lesson is not that all overlap should be merged. It is that grouping and rendering need separate diagnostics, and that a global renderer change can create new collisions.

A useful QA checklist is:

1. **Detection view**: show every text line, mask, confidence, orientation, and bubble candidate on the original. A reviewer must be able to see whether the error began at detection or association.
2. **Ownership view**: draw bubble contours and tails, then color each line by assigned bubble. Reject a merge that crosses a contour, changes orientation without evidence, or connects two tails.
3. **OCR view**: run whole-bubble and line-level OCR when confidence is low. Keep the original string, target string, and reading order. Multi-line Manga OCR is a useful whole-bubble option [community_failure_cases_and_a_practical_qa_checklist[2]] [6].
4. **Merge control**: offer split, merge, and three strength presets. The Android example's conservative, standard, and aggressive box merging is a practical interaction model [community_failure_cases_and_a_practical_qa_checklist[3]] [25].
5. **Translation view**: show target length, script direction, and glossary substitutions before rendering. If the target cannot fit, request a shorter alternative rather than silently shrinking below the readable minimum.
6. **Render view**: test actual glyph masks, not only AABBs. Flag overlap, page-boundary overflow, tail intersection, and line stacking. The issue report specifically identifies all four classes of failure [community_failure_cases_and_a_practical_qa_checklist[1]] [20].
7. **Removal view**: toggle the original, removed, and final layers. Check bubble borders, nearby panel art, and texture continuity.
8. **Regression set**: keep fixtures for adjacent balloons, touching balloons, open balloons, spiky balloons, vertical Japanese, furigana, captions, sound effects, tilted text, and one bubble containing two speakers. Record whether the system split, merged, or asked for review.

This workflow turns an embarrassing final image into a diagnosable pipeline result. The highest-value UI is often not another translation provider; it is a region editor that lets a reader correct ownership and layout without rerunning the entire page.
content.synthesis:
The major systems solve different problems, so comparing them as if they were competing translators is misleading.

| System or strategy | Mechanism | Scope | Main trade-off | Best role |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| manga-image-translator | detector, OCR, translation, mask/inpainting, and renderer pipeline [synthesis[0]] [10] | page-level rewritten images | broad control but complex grouping and typesetting failure modes [synthesis[0]] [10] | reference architecture for batch export |
| comic-text-detector | text boxes, lines, and text segmentation [synthesis[1]] [15] | text geometry only | useful masks but no documented speech-balloon ownership [synthesis[1]] [15] [synthesis[1]] [15] | front end to OCR, removal, and lettering |
| speech-balloon segmentation | pixel-wise balloon, carrier, and tail segmentation [synthesis[2]] [21] [synthesis[2]] [21] | semantic region ownership | needs a separate model and may be trained on a different comic domain | bubble and caption association |
| Google camera | automatic camera detection, NMT, offline models, and flicker stabilization [synthesis[3]] [11] | immediate camera/image comprehension | fast and polished but internally opaque for comic layout | preview benchmark |
| Android floating overlay | screenshot, OCR, translation, and movable overlay [synthesis[4]] [25] | live screen reading | reversible but source text and geometry remain runtime problems | mobile reader mode |
| inpainting export | mask-based pixel reconstruction [synthesis[5]] [16] | final image repair | clean output but mask and reconstruction errors are harder to undo | complex background cleanup |
| overlay export | separate rendered layer or bubble-shaped background [synthesis[6]] [7] [synthesis[4]] [25] | reversible preview | may cover art, drift, or let source text show through | review and rapid iteration |

The non-obvious tension is between semantic accuracy and visual quality. Merging adjacent boxes can help a language model reconstruct a sentence, but the same merge can combine two speakers. Enlarging a destination box can reduce clipping, but the issue evidence shows that it can create overlap. Inpainting can make a final page look clean, but a simple flat bubble often benefits from a deterministic fill that is easier to verify.

The recommended architecture is therefore a two-plane system. The semantic plane stores line instances, bubble ownership, OCR, translation, direction, and reading order. The pixel plane stores text masks, safe masks, background operations, shaped glyphs, and compositing layers. CTD supplies fine text geometry; a balloon or caption model supplies ownership; manga-image-translator-style mask and renderer controls supply export; Android-style adjustable overlays supply live review.

For implementation, adopt three defaults: do not merge without shared bubble evidence; do not fit to a text rectangle when a bubble mask is available; and do not make inpainting the only output. Provide a fast reversible overlay, a deterministic flat-fill path, and a learned inpainting path, all backed by the same region editor. This gives separate bubbles, readable rounded and spiky balloons, and a clean escalation path when automation is uncertain.
